4. A party of three men; three men or three personifications in company or forming one group; also, a trio or triad of any kind.

{{smaller block|Still purposing to grant no more then what seem'd good to that violent and lawless ''Triumvirate'' within him, under the falsifi'd names of his Reason, Honour, and Conscience.
{{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, xxii.}}}}

{{smaller block|Theology, Philosophy, and Science constitute our spiritual ''triumvirate''.
{{right|''G. H. Lewes'', Hist. Philos., I. p. xvii.}}}}

'''triumviri''', ''n.'' Latin plural of ''triumvir''.

'''triumviry†''' (trī-um′vi-ri), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''triumverie''; < ''triumvir'' + ''-y''<sup>3</sup>.] A triumvirate.

{{smaller block|Thou makest the ''triumviry'', the corner-cap of society.
{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., iv. 3. 53.}}}}

{{smaller block|Take for thine ayde afflicting Miserie,
Woe, mine attendant, and Dispayre, my freend,
All three my greatest great ''Triumuerie''.
{{right|''G. Markham'', Sir R. Grinuile, p. 55. (''Davies.'')}}}}

{{smaller block|We read in Scripture of a ''triune'' Deity.
{{right|''Bp. Burnet.''}}}}

'''Triune vase.''' {{smaller|Same as ''triple vase'' (which see, under ''vase'').}}

{{smaller block|Thou art . . . a trifler, a ''trivant'', thou art an idle fellow.

{{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 138.}}}}

'''trive†''', ''v. t.'' [Abbr. from ''contrive''<sup>1</sup>.] To contrive.

{{smaller block|The thrifty that teacheth the thriving to thrive,

{{right|''Tusser'', Husbandry, Brief Conclusion.}}}}

{{smaller block|The ''trivial'' round, the common task,
Would furnish all we ought to ask.
{{right|''Keble'', Christian Year, Morning.}}}}

{{smaller block|The ''triunity'' of the Godhead.
{{right|''Dr. H. More,'' Mystery of Godliness, p. 203. (''Latham.'')}}}}

'''Triurideæ''' (trī-ū-rid′ẹ̄-ē), ''n. pl.'' [NL. (Bentham and Hooker, 1883), < ''Triuris'' (''-urid-'') + ''-eæ.''] An order of monocotyledonous plants, of the series ''Apocarpeæ.'' {{smaller|It is characterized by unisexual racemose flowers with a regular perianth of three to eight valvate segments in a single row. It includes 2 genera, ''Triuris'' (the type) and ''Sciaphila,'' the latter comprising about 14 species of white or reddish plants of South America, India, the Malay archipelago, and Papua. The order is nearest akin to the ''Alismaceæ,'' but is terrestrial and saprophytic, growing upon decayed wood and leaves. Its species are diminutive, slender, but rather rigid leafless plants, wholly white, yellow, pink, or red, with a few scales at the base, and producing a few long flexuous unbranched roots. The small stellate flowers are numerous and racemose, or fewer and somewhat corymbose; they hang on decurved pedicels, and are often papillose or minutely fringed.}}

'''Triuris''' (trī-ū′ris), ''n.'' [NL. (Miers, 1841), so called with ref. to the appendaged calyx-lobes; < Gr. τρεῖς, three, + οὐρά, a tail.] A genus of plants, type of the order ''Triurideæ.'' {{smaller|It is characterized by anthers immersed in a large conical receptacle,}}

{{smaller block|He shulde fynde in one place a friyngpan, in an other a chauldron, here a ''tryuet,'' and there a spytte, and these in maner in euery pore mannes house.
{{right|''Peter Martyr'' (tr. in Eden's First Books on America, ed. [Arber, p. 145).}}}}

{{smaller block|She got up to set the pot of coffee back on the ''trivet.''
{{right|''E. Eggleston,'' The Graysons, xxxii.}}}}

2. In ''her.,'' a bearing representing the three-legged iron support used in cooking. {{smaller|It is usually represented in plan, or as looked at from above, the feet or uprights seen in perspective.—'''Right as a trivet,''' standing steadily (in allusion to the fact that a tripod stands firm on irregular surfaces); hence, proverbially, entirely or perfectly right. [Colloq.]}}

{{smaller block|I'll warrant you'll find yourself ''right as a trivet!''
{{right|''Barham,'' Ingoldsby Legends, II. 71.}}}}

{{smaller block|“As to the letter, Rokesmith,” said Mr. Boffin, “you're as ''right as a trivet.''” ''Dickens,'' Our Mutual Friend, ii. 14.}}

'''trivet'''<sup>2</sup> (triv′et), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''trevat;'' origin obscure.] A knife for cutting the loops of terry fabrics, such as velvets or Wilton carpets, in which the looped warp is formed over wires in the shed. {{smaller|Each wire has a groove at the top to serve as a guide for the trivet, which can be run rapidly along the wires, cutting all the loops and thus making a pile fabric or cut pile fabric. ''E. H. Knight.''}}

{{smaller block|For velvets, &c., the wires are provided with a groove on their upper face, and along this groove a cutting knife called a ''trivet'' is run to cut the loops.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.,'' XXIV. 467.}}}}

{{smaller block|The ''triviality'' of its meaningless details. ''J. Caird.''}}

2. Pl. ''trivialities'' (-tiz). A trivial thing; a trifle; a matter of little value or importance. ''Cotgrave.''

{{smaller block|It is in these acts called ''trivialities'' that the seeds of joy are forever wasted, until men and women look round with haggard faces at the devastation their own waste has made. ''George Eliot,'' Middlemarch, xlii.}}

'''trivialize''' (triv′i-a̤l-īz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''trivialized,'' ppr. ''trivializing.'' [< ''trivial'' + ''-ize.''] To render trivial or paltry.

{{smaller block|''Southey.'' . . . We are now at the Sonnets [of Milton]. I know your dislike of this composition.
''Landor.'' In English, not in Italian; but Milton has ennobled it in our tongue, and has ''trivialized'' it in that.
{{right|''Landor,'' Imag. Conv., Southey and Landor, ii.}}}}

'''trivially''' (triv′i-a̤l-i), ''adv.'' In a trivial manner.

{{smaller block|Neither is money the sinews of war (as it is ''trivially'' said).
{{right|''Bacon,'' True Greatness of Kingdoms, etc. (ed. 1887).}}}}

'''trivialness''' (triv′i-a̤l-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being trivial; triviality.

{{smaller block|We always seem to be living just on the brink of a pure and lofty intercourse, which would make the ills and ''trivialness'' of life ridiculous. ''Thoreau,'' Letters, p. 13.}}

[NL., < ''Trivia'' + ''-idæ.''] A family of involute tænioglossate gastropods, typified by the genus ''Trivia.'' {{smaller|They are of small size, and closely related to the cowries, but differ in the multicuspid median teeth and unguiform marginal teeth of the radula, and the shell is generally transversely}} and by a nearly or quite terminal style. The 2 species, ''T. hyalina'' and ''T. lutea'', are natives of Brazil.
